name: Tuberculosis (TB)
overview: Tuberculosis is a bacterial infection that mainly affects the lungs but can affect other parts of the body. It spreads through the air when someone with active TB in the lungs coughs. It is curable with a long course of antibiotics taken exactly as prescribed.
symptoms: A cough lasting more than 3 weeks, which may bring up mucus or blood
Weight loss and loss of appetite
Swellings in the neck or other glands
causes: Infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis bacteria
Breathing in bacteria from the coughs or sneezes of someone with active lung TB, usually after prolonged close contact
riskFactors: Close contact with someone with active TB
Living in or travelling to areas where TB is common
HIV or another cause of a weakened immune system
diagnosis: Doctors use a chest X-ray, tests on samples of mucus, and skin or blood tests to look for TB infection.
treatment: A combination of antibiotics taken for several months
Taking every dose for the full course to cure TB and prevent drug resistance
Treatment of latent TB to stop it becoming active in some people
selfCare: Take medicines exactly as prescribed
Cover your mouth when coughing and ventilate rooms while infectious
Eat well and avoid alcohol and smoking
prevention: BCG vaccine for people at higher risk, as offered
Screening and treatment of close contacts
Early diagnosis and full treatment of people with TB
whenToSeeDoctor: A cough lasting more than 3 weeks
Unexplained weight loss, fever or night sweats
You have been in close contact with someone with TB
emergencySigns: Coughing up a lot of blood
Severe headache with a stiff neck or confusion

name: Malaria
overview: Malaria is a serious infection caused by parasites spread through the bites of infected mosquitoes. It is common in parts of Africa, Asia and South and Central America. It can be life-threatening but is preventable and curable if treated promptly.
symptoms: Symptoms can appear weeks or even months after travel
causes: Plasmodium parasites passed on by the bite of infected Anopheles mosquitoes
Rarely, through blood transfusion or from mother to baby during pregnancy
riskFactors: Living in or travelling to areas where malaria is common
Not taking antimalarial tablets when advised
diagnosis: Malaria is diagnosed with a blood test, either under a microscope or with a rapid diagnostic test; mention any recent travel.
treatment: Antimalarial medicines prescribed by a doctor, chosen by the type of parasite and where it was caught
Hospital treatment for severe malaria
selfCare: Seek medical help urgently if you develop a fever during or after travel to a malaria area
Finish all medicines as prescribed
prevention: Get travel health advice before travelling
Antimalarial tablets if recommended
Use insect repellent, cover up and sleep under a mosquito net
Malaria vaccines for children in some high-risk countries
whenToSeeDoctor: Fever or flu-like symptoms during or within a year of visiting a malaria area: get medical help the same day
You are planning travel to a malaria area (get advice on prevention before you go)
emergencySigns: Yellowing of the skin or eyes with feeling very unwell
Dark urine or passing little urine

name: Dengue
overview: Dengue is a viral infection spread by mosquitoes in tropical and subtropical regions. Many people have no or mild symptoms, but a small number develop severe dengue, which needs urgent hospital care.
symptoms: Severe headache and pain behind the eyes
causes: Dengue virus passed on by bites of infected Aedes mosquitoes, which bite mainly during the day
The same mosquitoes can spread other infections such as Zika and chikungunya, which can cause similar symptoms
riskFactors: Living in or travelling to tropical and subtropical areas
Previous dengue infection (raises the risk of severe dengue with a second infection)
diagnosis: Dengue is diagnosed with blood tests, alongside your symptoms and travel history.
treatment: There is no specific antiviral treatment; care focuses on rest, fluids and paracetamol for pain and fever
Avoid aspirin and ibuprofen-type painkillers, which can increase bleeding risk
Hospital care for severe dengue
selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Use paracetamol rather than anti-inflammatory painkillers
Watch closely for warning signs as the fever goes down
prevention: Use insect repellent and cover up, especially during the day
Remove standing water where mosquitoes breed
Vaccination for some people, depending on country and past infection
whenToSeeDoctor: Fever during or after travel to an area with dengue
Symptoms not improving after a few days
emergencySigns: Bleeding gums or nose, or blood in vomit or stool
Restlessness, extreme tiredness or cold clammy skin

name: Hepatitis A
overview: Hepatitis A is a liver infection caused by a virus spread through contaminated food, water or close contact. It usually clears up on its own within a few months and does not cause long-term liver disease. A vaccine is available.
symptoms: Flu-like symptoms such as tiredness, fever and aches
Loss of appetite and feeling sick
Pain in the upper right tummy
Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice)
causes: Hepatitis A virus spread when tiny amounts of infected stool get into the mouth
Contaminated food or water, especially in areas with poor sanitation
Close contact with an infected person
riskFactors: Travel to areas where hepatitis A is common
Close contact with someone who has it
Men who have sex with men
diagnosis: Hepatitis A is diagnosed with a blood test.
treatment: No specific treatment; the infection usually clears on its own
Rest, fluids and relief of symptoms
Avoid alcohol and check with a doctor before taking medicines
selfCare: Rest and eat small, light meals
Avoid alcohol
Wash hands thoroughly and do not prepare food for others while infectious
prevention: Hepatitis A vaccine for travellers and people at higher risk
Wash hands after the toilet and before preparing food
Drink safe water when travelling
whenToSeeDoctor: Yellowing of the skin or eyes
Symptoms of hepatitis after travel or contact with an infected person

name: Hepatitis B
overview: Hepatitis B is a liver infection caused by a virus spread through blood and body fluids. Adults usually clear it within a few months, but it can become a long-term (chronic) infection, especially when caught in infancy. A safe and effective vaccine is available.
symptoms: Flu-like symptoms such as tiredness and fever
Yellowing of the skin or eyes (jaundice)
causes: Hepatitis B virus passed on through blood, semen and vaginal fluids
From mother to baby around birth
Unprotected sex or sharing needles
riskFactors: Being born to a mother with hepatitis B
Unprotected sex with an infected partner
Living in or coming from an area where hepatitis B is common
Unsterile tattooing, piercing or medical equipment
diagnosis: Hepatitis B is diagnosed with blood tests, which also show whether the infection is recent or chronic.
treatment: Short-term infections often need only symptom relief
Antiviral medicines for chronic hepatitis B to control the virus and protect the liver
Regular monitoring of liver health
selfCare: Avoid alcohol
Use condoms and do not share razors or toothbrushes
Attend regular check-ups
prevention: Hepatitis B vaccine, including for babies
Vaccination and treatment of babies born to mothers with hepatitis B
Use condoms and never share needles
whenToSeeDoctor: You may have been exposed (urgent vaccination can help prevent infection)
Symptoms of hepatitis such as jaundice
You are pregnant and have not been tested
emergencySigns: Vomiting blood or black, tarry stools

name: Hepatitis C
overview: Hepatitis C is a virus spread mainly through blood that can infect and damage the liver. It often causes no symptoms for many years. Modern antiviral tablets can cure most people.
symptoms: Yellowing of the skin or eyes in later stages
causes: Hepatitis C virus spread through blood-to-blood contact
Sharing needles or drug equipment
Unsterile tattooing, piercing or medical procedures
riskFactors: Injecting drugs, now or in the past
Blood transfusions or medical treatment in countries where screening is limited
Sharing razors or toothbrushes with an infected person
diagnosis: Hepatitis C is diagnosed with blood tests: an antibody test, then a test for the virus itself.
treatment: Antiviral tablets taken for several weeks, which cure most people
Monitoring and care for any liver damage
selfCare: Avoid alcohol
Do not share razors, toothbrushes or needles
Keep a healthy weight
prevention: Never share needles or drug equipment
Use licensed tattoo and piercing studios
Testing for people at higher risk
whenToSeeDoctor: You have ever been at risk of infection and have not been tested
Persistent tiredness or symptoms of liver problems

name: HIV
overview: HIV is a virus that damages the immune system. There is no cure, but effective treatment keeps the virus under control so people can live long, healthy lives. People on effective treatment with an undetectable viral load cannot pass HIV on through sex.
symptoms: Many people have no symptoms for years
A short flu-like illness a few weeks after infection: fever, sore throat and rash
Without treatment, later: weight loss, recurring infections, night sweats and swollen glands
causes: HIV passed on through blood, semen, vaginal and anal fluids, and breast milk
Most commonly through sex without a condom
Sharing needles
From mother to baby during pregnancy, birth or breastfeeding if untreated
riskFactors: Sex without a condom with a partner of unknown or detectable HIV status
diagnosis: HIV is diagnosed with a blood test or a finger-prick or saliva test; testing is free and confidential at sexual health clinics.
treatment: Antiretroviral medicines taken every day for life
Regular check-ups to monitor the immune system and viral load
selfCare: Take treatment every day as prescribed
Stay up to date with recommended vaccines
Keep a healthy lifestyle and attend check-ups
prevention: Use condoms
Pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) for people at higher risk
Post-exposure prophylaxis (PEP) within 72 hours of possible exposure
Never share needles
Regular testing
whenToSeeDoctor: You think you have been exposed to HIV (go within 72 hours for PEP)
You have had unprotected sex or shared needles and have not been tested
Flu-like illness after a possible exposure
emergencySigns: Very high fever with feeling extremely unwell

name: Chlamydia
overview: Chlamydia is one of the most common sexually transmitted infections. Most people have no symptoms, so testing is the only way to know. It is easily treated with antibiotics, but untreated it can cause long-term problems such as infertility.
symptoms: Unusual discharge from the vagina, penis or bottom
Pain in the tummy, bleeding after sex or between periods
Pain and swelling in the testicles
causes: Chlamydia trachomatis bacteria passed on through unprotected vaginal, anal or oral sex
Sharing sex toys
From mother to baby during birth
riskFactors: A new sexual partner or multiple partners
diagnosis: Chlamydia is diagnosed with a urine test or a swab, available at sexual health clinics, GPs and via home testing kits.
treatment: Antibiotics prescribed by a doctor or nurse
Avoid sex until you and your partner(s) have finished treatment
Partners should be tested and treated
selfCare: Finish the full course of antibiotics
Tell recent sexual partners so they can get tested
prevention: Use condoms
Regular STI testing, especially with new partners
whenToSeeDoctor: You have symptoms of an STI
A partner has an STI
You have had sex without a condom with a new partner
emergencySigns: Severe pain in one side of the lower tummy with a missed period (possible ectopic pregnancy)

name: Gonorrhoea
overview: Gonorrhoea is a sexually transmitted infection caused by bacteria. Many people have no symptoms. It is treated with antibiotics, but resistance to some antibiotics is a growing concern, so follow-up testing may be advised.
symptoms: Often no symptoms, especially in women
Thick green or yellow discharge from the vagina or penis
Pain or discomfort in the bottom
causes: Neisseria gonorrhoeae bacteria passed on through unprotected vaginal, oral or anal sex
Sharing sex toys
From mother to baby during birth
diagnosis: Gonorrhoea is diagnosed with a swab or urine test at a sexual health clinic or GP.
treatment: Antibiotics, usually given by injection, at a sexual health clinic
A follow-up test may be advised to confirm the infection has gone
Partners should be tested and treated
selfCare: Avoid sex until treatment is complete and you have been told the infection has cleared
Tell recent sexual partners
prevention: Use condoms
Regular STI testing
whenToSeeDoctor: You have symptoms of an STI
A partner has gonorrhoea
You have had unprotected sex with a new partner
emergencySigns: Hot, swollen, painful joints with fever and skin spots

name: Genital herpes
overview: Genital herpes is a common sexually transmitted infection caused by the herpes simplex virus. The virus stays in the body and can cause outbreaks of sores from time to time. There is no cure, but treatment can ease outbreaks and reduce how often they happen.
symptoms: Small blisters that burst to leave red, open sores around the genitals, bottom or thighs
Tingling, burning or itching around the genitals
Flu-like symptoms during the first outbreak
causes: Herpes simplex virus passed on through skin-to-skin contact during vaginal, anal or oral sex
Oral sex with someone who has a cold sore
diagnosis: A doctor or nurse at a sexual health clinic may diagnose herpes by looking at the sores and taking a swab.
treatment: Antiviral medicine to shorten outbreaks
Longer-term antiviral treatment for frequent outbreaks
Painkillers and soothing creams as advised
selfCare: Keep the area clean and dry
Apply ice wrapped in a cloth or petroleum jelly to sores
Pee in a bath or with water poured over the area to reduce pain
Avoid sex from first tingling until sores have fully healed
prevention: Use condoms or dental dams
Avoid sex during outbreaks
Avoid oral sex when you or a partner has a cold sore
whenToSeeDoctor: You think you have genital herpes
You are pregnant and have symptoms
Outbreaks are frequent or severe
emergencySigns: Severe headache with a stiff neck or confusion

name: HPV and genital warts
overview: HPV is a very common group of viruses spread through skin-to-skin contact, including during sex. Most infections cause no symptoms and clear on their own, but some types cause genital warts and others can lead to cancers such as cervical cancer. The HPV vaccine protects against the most harmful types.
symptoms: Genital warts: small, painless growths or lumps around the genitals or anus
causes: Human papillomavirus spread through skin-to-skin contact of the genital area
Vaginal, anal or oral sex and sharing sex toys
riskFactors: Smoking or a weakened immune system (harder to clear the virus)
diagnosis: Genital warts are diagnosed by examination at a sexual health clinic; high-risk HPV is checked through cervical screening.
treatment: Creams or liquids applied to warts, prescribed by a clinician
Freezing, heating or removing warts at a clinic
Follow-up of abnormal cervical screening results
selfCare: Do not use over-the-counter wart treatments meant for hands or feet on genital warts
Use condoms during treatment
prevention: HPV vaccination
Use condoms (reduces but does not fully remove risk)
Attend cervical screening when invited
whenToSeeDoctor: You notice lumps or growths around the genitals or anus
You are invited for cervical screening
Unusual bleeding, such as after sex or between periods

name: Syphilis
overview: Syphilis is a bacterial sexually transmitted infection. It often starts with a painless sore and can be easily missed. It is cured with antibiotics, but without treatment it can cause serious problems years later.
symptoms: A small, usually painless sore or ulcer on the genitals, anus or mouth
Later, a blotchy rash, often on the palms and soles
causes: Treponema pallidum bacteria passed on through close contact with a sore, usually during sex
From mother to baby during pregnancy
riskFactors: Men who have sex with men
diagnosis: Syphilis is diagnosed with a blood test and sometimes a swab from a sore, at a sexual health clinic.
treatment: Antibiotics, usually by injection
Follow-up blood tests to check treatment worked
Partners should be tested and treated
selfCare: Avoid sex until treatment is finished and sores have healed
Tell recent sexual partners
prevention: Use condoms
Regular STI testing
Screening in pregnancy
whenToSeeDoctor: A sore or rash on the genitals, anus or mouth
A partner has syphilis
You are pregnant and have not been screened

name: Whooping cough
overview: Whooping cough is a bacterial infection of the lungs and breathing tubes that causes long bouts of coughing. It can be very serious for young babies. Vaccination in pregnancy and childhood helps protect babies.
symptoms: Cold-like symptoms at first, such as runny nose and sore throat
Coughing bouts lasting a few minutes, worse at night
A 'whoop' sound when breathing in between coughs
Bringing up thick mucus or vomiting after coughing
Babies may not whoop but may stop breathing briefly or turn blue
causes: Bordetella pertussis bacteria
Spread through coughs and sneezes
riskFactors: Babies too young to be fully vaccinated
Close contact with someone with whooping cough
diagnosis: A doctor may suspect it from the cough and confirm it with a nose or throat swab or a blood test.
treatment: Antibiotics if diagnosed early, to reduce spread
Hospital treatment for babies with severe whooping cough
selfCare: Rest and drink plenty of fluids
Stay away from nursery, school or work until 48 hours after starting antibiotics, or 3 weeks after coughing started
Keep away from babies
prevention: Whooping cough vaccine in pregnancy to protect newborns
Routine childhood vaccinations
whenToSeeDoctor: A baby under 6 months has symptoms
Coughing bouts that are getting worse
You are pregnant and have been in contact with whooping cough
A cough that lasts for weeks
emergencySigns: Lips, tongue or skin turning blue or grey
Pauses in breathing or difficulty breathing
A baby who is floppy or unresponsive

name: Meningitis
overview: Meningitis is an infection of the protective layers around the brain and spinal cord. Bacterial meningitis is a medical emergency and can be life-threatening, while viral meningitis is usually milder. Vaccines protect against several causes.
symptoms: A rash that does not fade when a glass is rolled over it (not always present)
Stiff neck and dislike of bright lights
causes: Bacteria such as meningococcus or pneumococcus
Viruses
Spread by coughs, sneezes, kissing or close contact
riskFactors: Living in crowded settings such as student halls
diagnosis: Meningitis is diagnosed in hospital with blood tests and a lumbar puncture, where fluid is taken from the spine.
treatment: Urgent antibiotics in hospital for bacterial meningitis
Fluids, oxygen and other support in hospital
Viral meningitis usually gets better on its own with rest
selfCare: Do not wait for a rash to appear before getting help
Trust your instincts if someone seems seriously ill
prevention: Routine vaccines including MenB, MenACWY, Hib and pneumococcal
Antibiotics may be offered to close contacts of someone with bacterial meningitis
whenToSeeDoctor: Any suspicion of meningitis: get medical help immediately rather than waiting for a routine appointment
You have been in close contact with someone with bacterial meningitis
Ongoing problems such as hearing loss or headaches after recovery
emergencySigns: Rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it
Drowsiness, confusion or being hard to wake
In babies: a bulging soft spot, floppiness or a high-pitched cry

name: Sepsis
overview: Sepsis is a life-threatening reaction to an infection, where the body's response damages its own tissues and organs. It needs emergency treatment. It can start from any infection, such as a chest or urine infection.
symptoms: Acting confused, slurred speech or not making sense
Blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin, lips or tongue
A rash that does not fade when a glass is rolled over it
Difficulty breathing or very fast breathing
Fast heartbeat, high or very low temperature, shivering
causes: The body's overreaction to an infection, often of the lungs, urinary tract, tummy or skin
Infections from wounds, burns or recent surgery, or from medical devices such as catheters
riskFactors: Diabetes or a weakened immune system
Recent surgery, serious illness or wounds
diagnosis: Sepsis is diagnosed in hospital from checks of temperature, heart rate, breathing and blood pressure, plus blood tests.
treatment: Emergency treatment in hospital with antibiotics
Fluids given into a vein and oxygen
Intensive care support if organs are affected
selfCare: Do not wait: call emergency services if you suspect sepsis
Follow rehabilitation advice after recovery, as some people have lasting effects
prevention: Keep up to date with vaccinations
Treat infections promptly
Clean wounds and wash hands
whenToSeeDoctor: Feeling very unwell with an infection that is not improving or is getting worse
A child or adult with an infection who seems much more unwell than expected
emergencySigns: Confusion, slurred speech or not making sense
Blue, grey, pale or blotchy skin, lips or tongue
Rash that does not fade under a glass
Difficulty breathing or very fast breathing

name: Urinary tract infection (UTI)
overview: Urinary tract infections affect the bladder, urethra or kidneys. They are very common, especially in women. Mild bladder infections may get better on their own, but many are treated with antibiotics.
symptoms: Needing to pee more often or more urgently
Confusion or agitation in older people
causes: Bacteria, usually from the bowel, getting into the urethra and bladder
Things that make it easier for bacteria to enter or stay in the bladder, such as sex, catheters, or not emptying the bladder fully
riskFactors: Conditions that block the flow of urine, such as kidney stones or an enlarged prostate
diagnosis: A GP or pharmacist usually diagnoses a UTI from symptoms; a urine test may be used, especially for men, children, pregnant people or repeated infections.
treatment: Antibiotics prescribed by a doctor, nurse or pharmacist
Paracetamol or ibuprofen for pain
selfCare: Drink plenty of water to pee regularly
Rest
Avoid sex until you feel better
prevention: Wipe from front to back after using the toilet
Pee as soon as possible after sex
Drink enough fluids so urine is pale
Do not hold in pee
whenToSeeDoctor: You are a man, pregnant, or have a child with symptoms
Symptoms are not improving or keep coming back
Blood in your urine
Symptoms after surgery or with a catheter
emergencySigns: High temperature with shivering and pain in the back or side (possible kidney infection)
Not passing any urine all day

name: Lyme disease
overview: Lyme disease is a bacterial infection spread to humans by infected ticks. It is easier to treat if diagnosed early. The classic first sign is a circular red rash around a tick bite.
symptoms: A circular or oval rash around a tick bite, which may look like a bull's-eye and spreads over days
Flu-like symptoms such as high temperature, headache and tiredness
Later, if untreated: facial weakness, nerve pain or joint swelling
causes: Borrelia bacteria passed on by the bite of an infected tick
Ticks are found in grassy and wooded areas and are more active in spring and summer
riskFactors: Spending time in woodland, heath or long grass where ticks live
Not checking for and removing ticks promptly
diagnosis: A doctor can diagnose Lyme disease from the typical rash; blood tests may be used if there is no rash.
treatment: Antibiotics prescribed by a doctor, usually for a few weeks
Longer or intravenous antibiotics for some later-stage symptoms, guided by a specialist
selfCare: Remove ticks promptly with fine-tipped tweezers or a tick-removal tool, gripping close to the skin
Clean the bite area and watch for a rash over the following weeks
prevention: Cover skin and use insect repellent in tick areas
Keep to clear paths
Check skin and clothing for ticks after being outdoors
whenToSeeDoctor: A rash appears after a tick bite
Flu-like symptoms after a tick bite or time in tick areas
emergencySigns: Weakness of the face with severe headache or stiff neck
